title: A newborn
hookLine: a new person in the world: hold or picture a baby and let the newness land

lines: A FACE NOBODY HAS SEEN BEFORE.
cards: A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Behind one door, a room that held two people an hour ago now holds three. Someone small is crying, and nobody in the room minds at all.
Tiny fingers. A face nobody has seen before, anywhere, ever. A person who was not in the world yesterday, and now is.
Grown-ups who were exhausted a minute ago go quiet and stare. They aren't looking at a problem to solve. They're looking at something brand new.

teach.b: First, a mother who kept quiet. In the Gospel of Luke, shepherds come in from the fields to see a newborn lying in a manger, and they spread the word about what they'd been told of this child.
In the King James words: "all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The hearers wonder.
The mother keeps it, and ponders. Second, a poet's warning. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran's book of short teachings, a woman holding a baby asks about children.
The answer begins: "Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself."
Parents may give their children love, Gibran goes on, but not their thoughts, because children have thoughts of their own. A newborn isn't a copy. It's someone new.
Third, why a baby stops people. Much of a day is things met before: the same roads, the same faces, the same news.

teach.h: PROOF THE WORLD STILL MAKES NEW THINGS.
teach.b: A newborn is plain proof that the world is still making new things. Not new products. New people, with their own faces and their own thoughts to come.
Fourth, the baby you once were.
Not everyone has a baby to hold, and for some people the subject is tender. But whoever is listening was once that new: unknown, unnamed. The newness in that room was, once, yours.

how: Several traditions mark a birth with blessings, naming ceremonies and prayers of thanks; Luke's account of the shepherds and Mary, and Gibran's words on children in The Prophet, are two texts that look at a new life with wonder.

o: a fresh start you make by changing your habits
a brand-new person, nobody's copy, worth pondering
a person who has just been baptized into a faith

games.q: a new person in the world. tap the pairs.
p: spread the word about the child

s: in The Prophet, Gibran says children belong to their parents' thoughts
he says parents may give love but not their thoughts: children have thoughts of their own.
in Luke, Mary keeps these things and ponders them in her heart
the hearers wonder; she keeps it, and ponders.
today's practice needs a real baby in your arms
you can picture one, or picture yourself on your first day.

games.q: in The Prophet, a woman holding a baby asks about children. how does the answer begin?
games.why: Gibran begins: "Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself."

practice: If there's a baby in your arms, just look; if not, picture one, a child you know, a photo, or yourself on your first day, small and unnamed. Notice the hands, the tiny nails, the quick, shallow breathing, and let the newness land.
If you pray, you can keep this moment the way Mary did and ponder it; if you don't, stay with the wonder of someone new.

wordCard.voice: A newborn. A person who wasn't in the world yesterday: something to ponder, in Luke's telling, and nobody's copy, in Gibran's. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: new. Every face you know was once a face nobody had seen. Until tomorrow.
